questions.text: A sole proprietor architect hires three junior architects and two support staff. What is true about professional responsibility for their work?

options.text: The junior architects are personally responsible for all their work
The sole proprietor remains fully responsible as architect-of-record
Support staff bear equal liability with the principal architect
Responsibility is divided equally among all six people

rationale.a: Misunderstands the architect-of-record doctrine—junior architects working under an RLA remain accountable to that RLA, not individually responsible.
rationale.c: Confuses professional licensing with administrative roles—only licensed architects have professional responsibility; support staff have no liability for architectural decisions.
rationale.d: Falsely distributes accountability—the architect-of-record concentrates full responsibility in one person by law, not divided liability.
rationale.correct: Although the architect may assign work to employees, the architect-of-record remains fully responsible for all architectural documents issued under the architect's seal or authorized signature.
rationale.takeaway: The principal architect bears ultimate responsibility for all work bearing their seal, regardless of who produced or assisted with it.

questions.text: Comparing startup costs and expansion capacity, a sole proprietor has which advantage over corporate practice?

options.text: Higher capital requirements for corporate registration
Minimal startup costs and simpler registration procedures
Easier access to venture capital investment
Greater capacity to specialize in multiple disciplines

rationale.a: Reverses the advantage—while corporations do have higher registration costs, that is not why sole proprietors have lower costs; it is because of simpler procedures.
rationale.c: Contradicts the structure—sole proprietors cannot easily attract venture capital; investors prefer corporate structures with growth potential.
rationale.d: Confuses specialization with expansion—specialty knowledge is individual, not structural; sole proprietorships limit multi-discipline teams.
rationale.correct: Sole proprietorships have minimal startup costs and simpler registration procedures compared to corporations, though they lack the capacity to attract investment capital or easily expand operations.
rationale.takeaway: Sole proprietorships offer low startup costs because they skip corporate formation formalities, but this simplicity limits growth capacity.

questions.text: Which of the following is an advantage specific to sole proprietorship structure?

options.text: Protection from personal creditors
Complete autonomy in business decisions
Ability to transfer ownership automatically
Shared risk with other professionals

rationale.a: Reverses reality—sole proprietors have zero protection from creditors because of unlimited personal liability.
rationale.c: Mistakes the transfer mechanism—sole proprietorship ownership requires negotiation and transfer documentation; it never transfers automatically.
rationale.d: Contradicts the structure—sole proprietors bear individual risk entirely; they do not share risk with other professionals by definition.
rationale.correct: Advantages of sole proprietorship include complete autonomy in all business decisions, including project selection, fee structures, and client relationships without requiring consultation.
rationale.takeaway: Sole proprietors decide alone on fees, clients, and projects without consulting partners or boards—this independence is their key competitive advantage.

questions.text: What type of insurance is essential for a sole proprietor architect?

options.text: General business liability only
Professional liability coverage
Property insurance exclusively
Workers compensation only

rationale.a: Conflates insurance types—general business liability covers bodily injury and property damage, not professional errors or design negligence specific to architecture.
rationale.c: Addresses wrong risk—property insurance covers building damage or theft, not claims from faulty design or professional mistakes in architectural services.
rationale.d: Misses professional liability coverage—workers compensation covers employee injuries only; architects need liability coverage for their own professional conduct.
rationale.correct: Professional liability insurance is critical for sole proprietors as it protects both the architect and clients from claims arising from architectural negligence and professional errors.
rationale.takeaway: Professional liability insurance protects architects against negligence and error claims arising from architectural work, not just general business risks.

questions.text: Which government agencies must register a sole proprietor architect in the Philippines?

options.text: PRC and BAR only
DTI and PRC
SEC and PRC only
BOA and city government

rationale.a: Confuses lawyer registration (BAR) with architect registration. Architects are regulated by the PRC/BOA, not the Integrated Bar of the Philippines.
rationale.c: SEC registration is strictly for corporations and partnerships. Sole proprietors register their trade name with the DTI.
rationale.d: While architects are licensed by the BOA, sole proprietorships do not undergo a separate firm registration with the BOA. City government permits are for local operation, not professional entity registration.
rationale.correct: Under RA 9266, individual architects register their license with PRC/BOA. Sole proprietorship business names register with DTI. Unlike corporations, they do not register as a 'firm' with the BOA.
rationale.takeaway: Sole proprietors register with two primary professional/business agencies: DTI (for the business name) and PRC (for the individual professional credential).

questions.text: A sole proprietor's personal health crisis affects practice continuity. Why is this a significant disadvantage?

options.text: Corporate insurance will not cover the architect, leaving the practice vulnerable to financial instability
The practice automatically dissolves with the architect's incapacity
Clients cannot file claims against the practice, which may lead to loss of trust and future business opportunities
The Board of Architecture automatically appoints a successor, which may not align with the original vision of the practice

rationale.a: Conflates insurance types—corporate insurance is irrelevant to sole proprietors; the issue is structural termination, not insurance eligibility.
rationale.c: Contradicts legal reality—clients retain full claims against a sole proprietor's assets even during incapacity; liability persists.
rationale.d: Attributes false authority to BOA—regulatory bodies do not appoint successors; succession requires prior planning by the owner.
rationale.correct: The practice terminates upon the architect's death, incapacity, or retirement unless ownership is transferred, creating vulnerability when personal circumstances change.
rationale.takeaway: Unlike corporations, a sole proprietor's illness or incapacity stops the practice immediately because no one has authority to continue operations.

questions.text: Under RA 9266, what is the relationship between a sole proprietor's DTI registration and personal liability protection?

options.text: DTI registration provides a corporate veil protecting personal assets, which is a misunderstanding of the legal implications
DTI registration establishes legal recognition but does not shield personal liability
DTI registration eliminates all professional liability claims, which is incorrect as liability remains with the proprietor
DTI registration transfers liability to the government, which is a false assumption about the nature of business registration

rationale.a: Falsely equates sole proprietorship with corporate structure—DTI registration never creates a corporate veil; that protection exists only in corporations.
rationale.c: Mistakes registration for immunity—DTI registration is purely business registration; it eliminates no professional liability exposure whatsoever.
rationale.d: Inverts liability assignment—liability stays with the architect, not the government; DTI registration does not transfer responsibility.
rationale.correct: DTI registration with the firm name provides basic legal recognition of the sole proprietorship but does not shield the architect from personal liability exposure.
rationale.takeaway: DTI registration is administrative legality only—it does not reduce personal liability, which remains unlimited under sole proprietorship structure.

questions.text: What is the primary legal liability characteristic of a sole proprietorship?

options.text: Limited to business assets only
Shared equally with employees
Unlimited personal liability
Protected by corporate veil

rationale.a: Confuses sole proprietorship liability with limited liability—only corporations and LLCs limit liability to business assets; sole proprietors expose all personal property.
rationale.b: Incorrectly distributes liability among employees—employees do not share liability with the owner; the sole proprietor bears full responsibility.
rationale.d: Mistakes the protection structure—sole proprietorships explicitly lack a corporate veil, which is why personal liability is unlimited.
rationale.correct: Sole proprietors have unlimited personal liability, meaning the architect's personal assets are exposed to judgment claims without corporate protection.
rationale.takeaway: Sole proprietors risk personal assets in lawsuits because sole proprietorships lack the corporate veil that shields personal property from business claims.

questions.text: How does the continuity of a sole proprietorship practice differ from a corporate practice?

options.text: Sole proprietorships continue indefinitely after the architect's death, provided there is a legal successor appointed
Corporate practices require more frequent renewal, often involving complex regulatory compliance and documentation
Sole proprietorship continuity depends entirely on the individual architect
Both structures have identical succession procedures, ensuring seamless transition in leadership

rationale.a: Reverses the fundamental difference—sole proprietorships terminate upon death, while corporations survive the founder.
rationale.b: Confuses renewal frequency with continuity—renewal timing does not address whether the practice survives the owner's departure.
rationale.d: Incorrectly equates structures—corporations have automatic succession and continuity independent of founders; sole proprietorships require intentional transfer.
rationale.correct: The continuity of a sole proprietorship depends entirely on the architect's ability and willingness to continue; death, incapacity, or retirement terminates the practice unless ownership is transferred.
rationale.takeaway: Sole proprietorship practices end when the architect dies or becomes unable to work; corporations continue independent of individual founders.

questions.text: In a sole proprietorship, who retains ownership of architectural documents and plans?

options.text: The client who commissioned the work
The sole proprietor architect exclusively
Shared between architect and client
The Professional Regulation Commission

rationale.a: Confuses payment of fees with ownership transfer—clients who pay for architectural services do not automatically own the intellectual property unless explicitly agreed.
rationale.c: Mistakes the default ownership rule as shared—ownership is entirely with the architect by default; sharing requires a written assignment agreement.
rationale.d: Attributes ownership to a regulatory body—PRC oversees professional standards but has no ownership stake in architectural documents produced by practitioners.
rationale.correct: The architect retains copyright ownership but grants client perpetual use license upon full payment per standard practice (UAP SPP 206).
rationale.takeaway: Architects own their drawings and plans as intellectual property unless a written agreement transfers ownership to the client.
